notes.meaning: An angel carrying one of the bowls of judgment invites John to see what will happen to the corrupt city, pictured as an unfaithful woman. She sits over many waters, showing that her evil influence reaches across many nations. God promises that her pride and sin will not escape his final judgment.

Rulers of the earth joined this woman in her unfaithfulness to God, and ordinary people fell under her sway. They became spiritually drunk on her false teaching and wicked practices, losing their sense of right and wrong. Worldly systems often make sin look attractive and desirable to the masses.

The Spirit carries John into a desert, where he sees the woman seated on a bright red beast covered with insults against God. The beast has seven heads and ten horns, representing worldly political power. This image shows how false religion leans on and steers the brutal governments of the earth.

The woman is dressed like royalty in purple and scarlet robes and covered in glittering gold and pearls. In her hand she holds a golden cup that looks beautiful outside, but inside it is filled with idolatry and filthy sins. Outward splendor often hides inner rot.

A title is written openly across her forehead, calling her Babylon the Great, the mother of corrupt religions and abominations across the earth. In ancient times, shameful women often wore headbands with their names, and this title shows she has no shame in her sin. She is the source and leader of worldly rebellion against God.

John sees that the woman is drunk with the blood of God's holy people who faithfully testified about Jesus. She has slaughtered so many believers that she revels in their death. John is struck with complete astonishment at her sheer cruelty and pride.

The angel asks John why he is so surprised and promises to explain the hidden meaning of both the woman and the beast. God does not want his servants to remain confused or afraid in the face of evil. The explanation will show that God remains fully in control.

The angel explains that the beast once existed, disappeared, and will come up from the pit of destruction before meeting its final doom. Worldly people whose names were not written in the Book of Life before creation will be tricked into marveling at its return. God's true people are protected from falling for this great deception.

Understanding this vision requires spiritual wisdom given by God. The seven heads represent seven mountains where the woman sits, pointing to great centers of worldly power. Most traditional readers connect these with the famous seven hills of Rome.

differ.view: The seven mountains are symbolic of great world governments rather than literal hills.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The seven mountains are a direct historical reference to the well-known seven hills of the city of Rome.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The passage cannot point to the papacy because the original Greek word means mountains rather than hills, and Vatican City rests on only a single hill.

notes.meaning: The heads also stand for seven rulers or forms of government. Five had already fallen from power before John's day, one was ruling while John wrote, and another was yet to come for a brief time. Earthly kingdoms rise and fall under God's watchful eye.

differ.view: The five fallen kings represent past world empires (Egypt, Assyria, Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece), Rome is the one that is, and a future revived Roman empire is the seventh.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The kings are a historical line of Roman emperors, with the first five running from Augustus to Nero, Vespasian as the ruler in power, and Titus as the one who would reign only briefly.

notes.meaning: The beast itself counts as an eighth ruler that grows out of the previous seven and shares their evil character. Even though it rises with great terror, its end is already determined, and it is going straight into destruction. God has already decided the defeat of every enemy of his kingdom.

The ten horns are ten future kings who had not yet received their crowns in John's time. They will eventually receive royal authority to reign alongside the beast for a very short period. Human power is fleeting and strictly limited by God.

These rulers share one single goal, which is to hand their power, armies, and authority over to the beast. They willingly pool their resources to build up an evil worldly empire. Sin often unites people who would otherwise oppose one another.

These allied forces go to war against the Lamb, Jesus Christ, but the Lamb completely defeats them. He conquers because He is the supreme Lord of lords and King of kings, ruling over every earthly authority. His followers share in this victory as ones who have been called, chosen, and kept faithful to the end.

The angel explains that the waters beneath the prostitute represent crowds of people from every tribe, nation, and language. Her corrupt system has established deep control over societies all around the world. No matter how large a crowd follows error, God's truth remains unchanged.

The ten allied kings and the beast will eventually turn on the woman and hate her. They will strip away her riches, ruin her power, and burn her up like a captured city. Evil alliances always turn against each other in the end.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The woman represents unfaithful first-century Jerusalem, which was turned on and burned with fire by the Roman armies in AD 70.

notes.meaning: God puts it into the hearts of these kings to carry out his divine plan by uniting and giving their authority to the beast. Their agreement will last only until everything God has spoken comes to pass. Even when wicked rulers think they are acting on their own, God is guiding history to fulfill his word.

The angel finishes by identifying the woman as the great city ruling over the kings of the earth, which in John's day was Rome. Her worldly reign looks unshakable to human eyes, but she faces certain judgment from God. Christians can trust that no earthly empire will outlast the kingdom of God.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The city can only refer to ancient pagan Rome or apostate Jerusalem, because the text speaks of a power that killed the first-century apostles and prophets.
